prize_parts.citation: For the development of ligand-controlled palladium-catalyzed carbon-nitrogen bond formation

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B011 alone, Buchwald and Hartwig. In answer to the chair's first question, the one-sentence difference from Heck, Negishi and Suzuki is that forming a C-N bond needs amine binding, deprotonation to a Pd-amido complex and a C-N reductive elimination that is intrinsically hard, and the general method exists only because bulky, electron-rich phosphine and carbene ligands were designed to force that step; this is a different mechanistic problem with a different solution, not the same reaction with another nucleophile. That is why I now propose a citation that names C-N bond formation and ligand control explicitly, so that it cannot be read as a second cross-coupling prize. The remaining case is unchanged and can be checked in the literature: more than 25 years of independent confirmation, routine use in total synthesis, medicinal chemistry and process routes, and a clean two-person attribution that no other shortlisted candidate matches. Round 1 strengthened my view on one point: four members converged on exactly the same two names and near-identical wording, and no member raised a maturity concern.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains the 2010 prize and the risk that the Academy sees a heteroatom extension. I hold that this is a judgement about novelty and not about merit, and the citation wording is my answer to it. The second objection is Kosugi: his tin-amide coupling is a real precursor, but it was stoichiometric in tin, narrow in scope and not a general method, so I keep him in the scientific background and out of the citation. Third, B068 has the widest opening base (seven of eight ranked it) and is a new capability, destroying a protein with a small molecule, rather than a better route to a bond chemists already make. If the committee decides that opening a new area outweighs completing a mature one, that is a defensible choice, but it needs a settled three-name citation first, and I have not yet seen one.

responses.point: Andrei argues that degradation gives chemists a new capability, destroying a protein with a small molecule, whereas C-N coupling is a better route to a bond already made, and he would accept B011 only as a second choice.
responses.response: That is the best statement of the case for B068, and I take it seriously. But a better route to a bond that is already made understates what happened: before 1995 aryl amines of this kind could not be made reliably and broadly, and the ligand-controlled method opened substrate classes that had been out of reach, which is a new capability for synthetic chemists. I also note your own admission that your case is stronger on novelty than on attribution; the committee cannot vote for a citation that does not yet exist. Your PROTAC-and-ligase trio (Crews, Deshaies, Ciulli) leaves out Handa and the glue strand, and I cannot tell whether that is one discovery or two. I would hold the ranking, but note that your willingness to accept B011 as a second choice matters for reaching five votes.

responses.point: Daniel ranks targeted protein degradation first as an original, general design principle that makes undruggable proteins targetable, and treats the missing approved degrader as a possible underweighting on his part.
responses.response: In reply to the chair's question on evidence: what would move me is either an approved degrader, which would show the chemistry carries into practice, or a committee-agreed citation that treats PROTACs and cereblon glues as one discovery with a defensible third name beside Crews and Deshaies. Handa and Ciulli are different choices, one for the glue strand and one for the PROTAC-ligand and ternary-complex strand, and I cannot see which is decisive. I still think much of the chemistry is recruitment of existing ligase biology by bifunctional molecules, but your point that the principle itself is new is fair and I do not dismiss it. For now, B068 stays as my first alternative and not my preference.

responses.point: Heiner asks the B011 supporters to state in one sentence what is new relative to Heck, Negishi and Suzuki, and whether the citation should name C-N bond formation and ligand design, and he would credit Kosugi only in the narrative.
responses.response: I answer in the case for: different elementary steps (amido formation and C-N reductive elimination), and a ligand-design solution that the C-C chemistry did not require. I agree the citation should say so, and I have changed my wording to name C-N bond formation and ligand control. On Kosugi, I have no evidence that the tin-amide reaction was closer to the general method than I described; it needed stoichiometric toxic tin reagents and was limited in scope, so I keep him in the background. I also agree with your concern that the 2010 overlap is not minor for the committee as a whole, and I withdraw the word minor.

responses.point: Xiaodong pairs B011 with a second part for nitrogenase (B003) with Rees alone credited for structure, and says the citation must be about C-N bond formation with ligand design, not cross-coupling again.
responses.response: I accept your wording point and have adopted it. I do not support the second part. Rees alone leaves out Einsle, who solved the high-resolution carbide structure, and Seefeldt, Dean and Ribbe, who established the biochemistry, and you yourself note that the mechanism and N2 binding site are unresolved, so the citation would rest on structure alone. Two parts of unequal weight would also look arbitrary. B011 stands on its own with two names and I would not trade a clean attribution for a second part. I would reconsider if the committee found a defensible two-name credit for the nitrogenase structure, but I do not see one now.

responses.point: Emma accepts the merit of B011 but asks for balance, since it is a third or fourth synthetic-methodology prize in a short period, and would not oppose it as part of a two-part prize; she prefers B019.
responses.response: I think the balance argument is fair as a matter for the committee, but it is not a scientific reason to defer a method whose merit you accept. Opening support is also not my argument for novelty; the ligand-design and mechanism case above is. On B019, I find phase separation an interesting physical-chemical principle, but you concede that physiological relevance is contested and that the credit cannot be cut cleanly at three, so on my own maturity and attribution tests I cannot rank it above B011. On a two-part prize, I would see B011 with B068 as more natural than a mismatch with B019, but only once B068 has a settled citation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that C-N coupling is conceptually distinct from the 2010 prize, which is the main factor that could keep B011 below five votes.
Whether B068 can settle a defensible three-name citation across the PROTAC and cereblon glue strands, or gains an approved degrader, in time to compete.
Whether the Academy would prefer a mature, universally used method over a newer modality with broader but shallower support.
Whether any new evidence about Kosugi's tin-amide work would justify adding him as a third name, although I currently find none.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal. None of the shortlisted candidates has a link to my institutions (Chalmers, KTH, Lund, Tartu) or to my mentor Masamune. As the committee's only synthetic organic chemist, I am an interested reader of B011 and I am aware of a possible bias toward it; I have tried to counter this by stating explicitly what would move me to B068. Lund colleagues Linke and Sparr are noted, with no collaboration with either on any candidate.
